blocks.text: In Prosorov’s house. A sitting-room with pillars; behind is seen a large dining-room. It is midday, the sun is shining brightly outside. In the dining-room the table is being laid for lunch.

It’s so warm today that we can keep the windows open, though the birches are not yet in flower. Father was put in command of a brigade, and he rode out of Moscow with us eleven years ago. I remember perfectly that it was early in May and that everything in Moscow was flowering then. It was warm too, everything was bathed in sunshine. Eleven years have gone, and I remember everything as if we rode out only yesterday. Oh, God! When I awoke this morning and saw all the light and the spring, joy entered my heart, and I longed passionately to go home.
Will you take a bet on it?
To go away to Moscow. To sell the house, drop everything here, and go to Moscow﻿ ﻿…
Yes! To Moscow, and as soon as possible.
I expect Andrey will become a professor, but still, he won’t want to live here. Only poor Masha must go on living here.
Masha can come to Moscow every year, for the whole summer.

Oh, he’s all right, but there’s his wife, his mother-in-law, and two daughters. This is his second wife. He pays calls and tells everybody that he’s got a wife and two daughters. He’ll tell you so here. The wife isn’t all there, she does her hair like a flapper and gushes extremely. She talks philosophy and tries to commit suicide every now and again, apparently in order to annoy her husband. I should have left her long ago, but he bears up patiently, and just grumbles.
Reads a newspaper as he walks.
Makes a note in his pocket diary.
What does my own little girl want?
Ivan Romanovitch, dear Ivan Romanovitch! I feel as if I were sailing under the broad blue sky with great white birds around me. Why is that? Why?

When I woke up today and got up and dressed myself, I suddenly began to feel as if everything in this life was open to me, and that I knew how I must live. Dear Ivan Romanovitch, I know everything. A man must work, toil in the sweat of his brow, whoever he may be, for that is the meaning and object of his life, his happiness, his enthusiasm. How fine it is to be a workman who gets up at daybreak and breaks stones in the street, or a shepherd, or a schoolmaster, who teaches children, or an engine-driver on the railway.﻿ ﻿… My God, let alone a man, it’s better to be an ox, or just a horse, so long as it can work, than a young woman who wakes up at twelve o’clock, has her coffee in bed, and then spends two hours dressing.﻿ ﻿… Oh it’s awful! Sometimes when it’s hot, your thirst can be just as tiresome as my need for work. And if I don’t get up early in future and work, Ivan Romanovitch, then you may refuse me your friendship.
You’re so used to seeing me as a little girl that it seems queer to you when my face is serious. I’m twenty!

How well I can understand that craving for work, oh God! I’ve never worked once in my life. I was born in Petersburg, a chilly, lazy place, in a family which never knew what work or worry meant. I remember that when I used to come home from my regiment, a footman used to have to pull off my boots while I fidgeted and my mother looked on in adoration and wondered why other people didn’t see me in the same light. They shielded me from work; but only just in time! A new age is dawning, the people are marching on us all, a powerful, health-giving storm is gathering, it is drawing near, soon it will be upon us and it will drive away laziness, indifference, the prejudice against labour, and rotten dullness from our society. I shall work, and in twenty-five or thirty years, every man will have to work. Everyone!
Takes a scent-bottle out of his pocket and sprinkles his chest and hands.
Takes another newspaper out of his pocket.
Somebody is heard tapping on the floor from below.
Yes, he looked so pleased as he went out that I’m pretty certain he’ll bring you a present in a moment.
Yes, it’s awful. He’s always doing silly things.
“There stands a green oak by the sea. And a chain of bright gold is around it﻿ ﻿… And a chain of bright gold is around it.﻿ ﻿…”
When a man talks philosophy, well, it is philosophy or at any rate sophistry; but when a woman, or two women, talk philosophy﻿—it’s all my eye.
What do you mean by that, you very awful man?
Give him a pie, nurse. Ferapont, go, she’ll give you a pie.
I don’t like this Mihail Potapitch or Ivanitch, Protopopov. We oughtn’t to invite him here.
Covers her face with her hands.
Exit into the dining-room, to the table.
My dear Ivan Romanovitch, what are you doing!
Ivan Romanovitch, you are simply shameless!
But your presents are so expensive!
The orderly goes into the dining-room with the samovar.
Please sit down. We’re very glad you’ve come.
From Moscow? Are you from Moscow?
I take it that you are Olga Sergeyevna, the eldest, and that you are Maria﻿ ﻿… and you are Irina, the youngest.﻿ ﻿…

Yes. I went to school in Moscow and began my service there; I was there for a long time until at last I got my battery and moved over here, as you see. I don’t really remember you, I only remember that there used to be three sisters. I remember your father well; I have only to shut my eyes to see him as he was. I used to come to your house in Moscow.﻿ ﻿…
I used to think I remembered everybody, but﻿ ﻿…
Alexander Ignateyevitch, you’ve come from Moscow. That is really quite a surprise!
We are going to live there, you see.
Yes, when they used to call me the lovelorn Major, I was young and in love. I’ve grown out of both now.
But you haven’t a single white hair yet. You’re older, but you’re not yet old.
I’m forty-two, anyway. Have you been away from Moscow long?
It’s all right. And where did you live?
Yes, but it’s so cold. It’s very cold here, and the midges.﻿ ﻿…

What are you saying! Here you’ve got such a fine healthy Russian climate. You’ve a forest, a river﻿ ﻿… and birches. Dear, modest birches, I like them more than any other tree. It’s good to live here. Only it’s odd that the railway station should be thirteen miles away.﻿ ﻿… Nobody knows why.
Now I know who you are. I remember.
I used to know your mother.
She was a good woman, rest her soul.
Do you know, I’m beginning to forget her face. We’ll be forgotten in just the same way.
Who knows? But on the other hand, they may call our life noble and honour its memory. We’ve abolished torture and capital punishment, we live in security, but how much suffering there is still!
He’s the learned member of the family. I expect he will be a professor some day. Father was a soldier, but his son chose an academic career for himself.
We ragged him today. We think he’s a little in love.
To a local lady. She will probably come here today.
Just think, Alexander Ignateyevitch comes from Moscow.
That’s all right. Now my little sisters won’t give you any rest.
I’ve already managed to bore your sisters.
Looks at the frame and does not know what to say.
Andrey waves his hand and walks away.

He’s got a degree, and plays the violin, and cuts all sorts of things out of wood, and is really a domestic Admirable Crichton. Don’t go away, Andrey! He’s got into a habit of always going away. Come here!
You are funny. Alexander Ignateyevitch used to be called the lovelorn Major, but he never minded.
I’d like to call you the lovelorn fiddler!
He’s in love! little Andrey is in love!
Roars with laughter, then sits down and reads a newspaper which he takes out of his pocket.

Yes father, rest his soul, educated us almost violently. It may seem funny and silly, but it’s nevertheless true, that after his death I began to fill out and get rounder, as if my body had had some great pressure taken off it. Thanks to father, my sisters and I know French, German, and English, and Irina knows Italian as well. But we paid dearly for it all!
A knowledge of three languages is an unnecessary luxury in this town. It isn’t even a luxury but a sort of useless extra, like a sixth finger. We know a lot too much.
You say that many years later on, life on this earth will be beautiful and wonderful. That’s true. But to share in it now, even though at a distance, we must prepare by work.﻿ ﻿…
Feci quod potui, faciant meliora potentes.
But you gave me one of these at Easter.
Must you go? No, not yet?
You’ll stop and have lunch with us. Please do.
Looks at the clock, then at his watch.
Let’s go and have lunch! There’s to be a masterpiece of baking!
Puts his paper into his pocket, and combs his beard.
Oh, that’s all right. I haven’t been drunk for two years. And it’s all the same, anyway!
Angrily, but so that her husband should not hear.
I shouldn’t go if I were you.﻿ ﻿… It’s quite simple.
Vassili Vassilevitch, that’s enough. Be quiet!
Masha’s out of sorts today. She married when she was eighteen, when he seemed to her the wisest of men. And now it’s different. He’s the kindest man, but not the wisest.
Enters and goes to the table.
I don’t like this Soleni of yours and I’m afraid of him. He only says silly things.
Nicolai Lvovitch, don’t speak to me of love.
Carefully examines herself in a mirror, and puts herself straight.
Kisses her firmly and at length.
Happy returns. I’m awfully shy, you’ve so many people here.
Is it a sign of anything?
No, it simply doesn’t go well﻿ ﻿… and it looks so queer.
They have all sat down to lunch in the dining-room, the sitting-room is empty.
I wish you a nice fiancée, Irina. It’s quite time you married.
Natalia Ivanovna, I wish you the same.
Natalia Ivanovna has a fiancé already.
Raps with her fork on a plate.
You’ve lost three good conduct marks.
This is a nice drink. What’s it made of?
There is to be a roast turkey and a sweet apple pie for dinner. Thank goodness I can spend all day and the evening at home. You’ll come in the evening, ladies and gentlemen.﻿ ﻿…
And please may I come in the evening!
They don’t stand on ceremony here.
They take the basket and go into the dining-room, where they have a noisy reception.
Takes a humming-top out of his pocket.
“There stands a green oak by the sea, And a chain of bright gold is around it﻿ ﻿… And a chain of bright gold is around it﻿ ﻿…”
Tearfully. What am I saying that for? I’ve had those words running in my head all day.﻿ ﻿…
I’m a hardened sinner, but I really don’t see why Natalia Ivanovna should blush.﻿ ﻿…
Don’t pay any attention to them! Wait﻿ ﻿… do stop, please.﻿ ﻿…
Covers her face with her hands.
I’m so unaccustomed to meeting people!
Two officers come in and, seeing the lovers kiss, stop in astonishment.
Scene as before. It is 8 p.m. Somebody is heard playing a concertina outside in the street. There is no fire.
She opens another door, and looks in, then closes it.
It’s all right, Natasha. The boy is well.
Still, I think we ought to put him on a diet. I am so afraid. And the entertainers were to be here after nine; they had better not come, Audrey.
I don’t know. After all, they were asked.

This morning, when the little boy woke up and saw me he suddenly smiled; that means he knew me. “Good morning, Bobby!” I said, “good morning, darling.” And he laughed. Children understand, they understand very well. So I’ll tell them, Andrey dear, not to receive the entertainers.
I was just thinking.﻿ ﻿… There is really nothing to say.﻿ ﻿…
Yes﻿ ﻿… there was something I wanted to tell you.﻿ ﻿… Oh, yes. Ferapont has come from the Council offices, he wants to see you.
Good morning, grandfather. What have you to say?
Hands him a book and a packet.
Thank you. It’s all right. Why couldn’t you come earlier? It’s past eight now.
I can’t tell﻿ ﻿… I’m hard of hearing.﻿ ﻿…

If you weren’t, I don’t suppose I should talk to you. I’ve got to talk to somebody, and my wife doesn’t understand me, and I’m a bit afraid of my sisters﻿—I don’t know why unless it is that they may make fun of me and make me feel ashamed﻿ ﻿… I don’t drink, I don’t like public-houses, but how I should like to be sitting just now in Tyestov’s place in Moscow, or at the Great Moscow, old fellow!

Moscow? That’s where a contractor was once telling that some merchants or other were eating pancakes; one ate forty pancakes and he went and died, he was saying. Either forty or fifty, I forget which.

In Moscow you can sit in an enormous restaurant where you don’t know anybody and where nobody knows you, and you don’t feel all the same that you’re a stranger. And here you know everybody and everybody knows you, and you’re a stranger﻿ ﻿… and a lonely stranger.
What? And the same contractor was telling﻿—perhaps he was lying﻿—that there was a cable stretching right across Moscow.
I can’t tell. The contractor said so.
Stretches himself and slowly goes into his own room.
I’m thirsty. I should like some tea.

I don’t speak of my husband, I’ve grown used to him, but civilians in general are so often coarse, impolite, uneducated. Their rudeness offends me, it angers me. I suffer when I see that a man isn’t quite sufficiently refined, or delicate, or polite. I simply suffer agonies when I happen to be among schoolmasters, my husband’s colleagues.

Yes.﻿ ﻿… It seems to me that civilians and army men are equally interesting, in this town, at any rate. It’s all the same! If you listen to a member of the local intelligentsia, whether to civilian or military, he will tell you that he’s sick of his wife, sick of his house, sick of his estate, sick of his horses.﻿ ﻿… We Russians are extremely gifted in the direction of thinking on an exalted plane, but, tell me, why do we aim so low in real life? Why?
Why is a Russian sick of his children, sick of his wife? And why are his wife and children sick of him?
What a noise in the oven. Just before father’s death there was a noise in the pipe, just like that.
I love you, love you, love you﻿ ﻿… I love your eyes, your movements, I dream of them.﻿ ﻿… Splendid, wonderful woman!
Covers her face with her hands.

My surname is really triple. I am called Baron Tuzenbach-Krone-Altschauer, but I am Russian and Orthodox, the same as you. There is very little German left in me, unless perhaps it is the patience and the obstinacy with which I bore you. I see you home every night.
I am tired. No, I don’t like the telegraph office, I don’t like it.
That’s the way she does her hair.
Only Natasha mustn’t get to know of these losses.
I expect it will be all the same to her.
Here he is.﻿ ﻿… Has he paid his rent?
Why are you so silent, Alexander Ignateyevitch?
I don’t know. I want some tea. Half my life for a tumbler of tea: I haven’t had anything since morning.
Well, if we can’t have any tea, let’s philosophize, at any rate.
About what? Let us meditate﻿ ﻿… about life as it will be after our time; for example, in two or three hundred years.

Well? After our time people will fly about in balloons, the cut of one’s coat will change, perhaps they’ll discover a sixth sense and develop it, but life will remain the same, laborious, mysterious, and happy. And in a thousand years’ time, people will still be sighing: “Life is hard!”﻿—and at the same time they’ll be just as afraid of death, and unwilling to meet it, as we are.
I don’t know. I’ve been laughing all day, ever since morning.
According to you, one should not even think about happiness! But suppose I am happy!
Still, I am sorry that my youth has gone.
Gogol says: life in this world is a dull matter, my masters!
And I say it’s difficult to argue with you, my masters! Hang it all.
The die is cast. I’ve handed in my resignation, Maria Sergeyevna.
So I heard. I don’t see what good it is; I don’t like civilians.
Takes the pencils and the knife, then, with joy.
And I bought myself a knife﻿ ﻿… look at it﻿ ﻿… one blade, another, a third, an ear-scoop, scissors, nail-cleaners.
Yes. I’m tired of winter. I’ve already forgotten what summer’s like.
It’s coming out, I see. We’re going to Moscow.
Bring some here, nurse. I shan’t go over there.
Takes his tumbler into the drawing-room and sits in a corner.
Covers her face in her hands.
He’s lucky who doesn’t notice whether it’s winter now, or summer. I think that if I were in Moscow, I shouldn’t mind about the weather.

A few days ago I was reading the prison diary of a French minister. He had been sentenced on account of the Panama scandal. With what joy, what delight, he speaks of the birds he saw through the prison windows, which he had never noticed while he was a minister. Now, of course, that he is at liberty, he notices birds no more than he did before. When you go to live in Moscow you’ll not notice it, in just the same way. There can be no happiness for us, it only exists in our wishes.
Takes cardboard box from the table.
What is it? Is it a secret?
Where has he gone? And I’d served tea.﻿ ﻿… What a man.
Goes to the table with her cup.
My dear! Why are you offended!
In the dining-room, by the table angrily.
Disturbs the cards on the table.
If I am cross, then don’t talk to me. Don’t touch me!
Don’t touch her, don’t touch her.﻿ ﻿…
You’re sixty, but you’re like a boy, always up to some beastly nonsense.
Je vous prie, pardonnez moi, Marie, mais vous avez des manières un peu grossières.
Il parait, que mon Bobick déjà ne dort pas
Home. Something extraordinary has happened to his wife again.
Why make peace? I haven’t quarrelled with you.
You always make me feel as if something has taken place between us. You’ve a strange character, you must admit.

When I’m with one other man I behave just like everybody else, but in company I’m dull and shy and﻿ ﻿… talk all manner of rubbish. But I’m more honest and more honourable than very, very many people. And I can prove it.
I often get angry with you, you always fasten on to me in company, but I like you all the same. I’m going to drink my fill tonight, whatever happens. Drink, now!
Takes a scent-bottle from his pocket, and scents his hands.
I’ve sent in my resignation. Basta! I’ve been thinking about it for five years, and at last made up my mind. I shall work.
No, my angel. Chehartma isn’t onion, but roast mutton.
And I tell you, chehartma﻿—is a sort of onion.
And I tell you, chehartma﻿—is mutton.
And I tell you, cheremsha﻿—is a sort of onion.
What’s the use of arguing! You’ve never been in the Caucasus, and never ate any chehartma.
I never ate it, because I hate it. It smells like garlic.
They promised for about nine; that is, quite soon.
“Oh my house, my house, my new-built house.”
Which one? There are two universities in Moscow.
Don’t care if there are three. So much the better.
Goes to the piano and plays a waltz.
Time for us to go. Goodbye.
Good night. It’s time we went.
What a shame! I was expecting to spend the evening here, but of course, if the little baby is ill﻿ ﻿… I’ll bring him some toys tomorrow.
Let’s go into the street, we can talk there. Then we can settle things.
I never managed to get married because my life flashed by like lightning, and because I was madly in love with your mother, who was married.
One shouldn’t marry. One shouldn’t, because it’s dull.
So there I am, in my loneliness. Say what you will, loneliness is a terrible thing, old fellow.﻿ ﻿… Though really﻿ ﻿… of course, it absolutely doesn’t matter!
What are you in such a hurry for? We shall be in time.
I’m afraid my wife may stop me.
I shan’t play tonight, I shall only sit and look on. I don’t feel very well.﻿ ﻿… What am I to do for my asthma, Ivan Romanovitch?
Don’t ask me! I don’t remember, old fellow, I don’t know.
A bell rings, then a second time; voices and laughter are heard.
Tell them there’s nobody at home, nurse. They must excuse us.
How strange. Are you here alone?

Just now I behaved tactlessly, with insufficient reserve. But you are not like all the others, you are noble and pure, you can see the truth.﻿ ﻿… You alone can understand me. I love you, deeply, beyond measure, I love you.
Here’s Andrey. Let him go on reading. Excuse me, Vassili Vassilevitch, I did not know you were here; I am engaged in domesticities.

Yes, but restlessly. By the way, dear, I wanted to tell you, but either you weren’t at home, or I was busy﻿ ﻿… I think Bobby’s present nursery is cold and damp. And your room would be so nice for the child. My dear, darling girl, do change over to Olga’s for a bit!
The bells of a troika are heard as it drives up to the house.
Well, there you are. And you said there was going to be a party.
It’s queer; I went away not long ago, half an hour ago, and they were expecting entertainers.
Has Masha gone too? Where has she gone? And what’s Protopopov waiting for downstairs in his troika? Whom is he expecting?

My wife took it into her head to frighten me just now by nearly poisoning herself. It’s all right now, and I’m glad; I can rest now.﻿ ﻿… But perhaps we ought to go away? Well, my best wishes, Feodor Ilitch, let’s go somewhere together! I can’t, I absolutely can’t stop at home.﻿ ﻿… Come on!
A concertina is being played in the street. The nurse sings.
In fur coat and cap, steps across the dining-room, followed by the maid.

The room shared by Olga and Irina. Beds, screened off, on the right and left. It is past 2 a.m. Behind the stage a fire-alarm is ringing; it has apparently been going for some time. Nobody in the house has gone to bed yet.

Now they are downstairs, sitting under the stairs. I said to them, “Won’t you come up,” I said, “you can’t go on like this,” and they simply cried, “We don’t know where father is.” They said, “He may be burnt up by now.” What an idea! And in the yard there are some people﻿ ﻿… also undressed.
Takes a dress out of the cupboard.
Couldn’t you call Ferapont, Olga dear. I can hardly manage.﻿ ﻿…
Through the open door can be seen a window, red with flame: afire-engine is heard passing the house.
Yes’m. In the year twelve Moscow was burning too. Oh, my God! The Frenchmen were surprised.

Nurse, dear, let them have everything. We don’t want anything. Give it all to them, nurse.﻿ ﻿… I’m tired, I can hardly keep on my legs.﻿ ﻿… The Vershinins mustn’t be allowed to go home.﻿ ﻿… The girls can sleep in the drawing-room, and Alexander Ignateyevitch can go downstairs to the Baron’s flat﻿ ﻿… Fedotik can go there, too, or else into our dining-room.﻿ ﻿… The doctor is drunk, beastly drunk, as if on purpose, so nobody can go to him. Vershinin’s wife, too, may go into the drawing-room.
You’re talking nonsense, nurse. Nobody is dismissing you.

They are saying that a committee to assist the sufferers from the fire must be formed at once. What do you think of that? It’s a beautiful idea. Of course the poor ought to be helped, it’s the duty of the rich. Bobby and little Sophy are sleeping, sleeping as if nothing at all was the matter. There’s such a lot of people here, the place is full of them, wherever you go. There’s influenza in the town now. I’m afraid the children may catch it.
They’ll appoint you, Olga. It’s settled.
Remember, dear﻿ ﻿… we have been brought up, in an unusual way, perhaps, but I can’t bear this. Such behaviour has a bad effect on me, I get ill﻿ ﻿… I simply lose heart!
Even the least bit of rudeness, the slightest impoliteness, upsets me.
I often say too much, it’s true, but you must agree, dear, that she could just as well live in the country.
She has been with us for thirty years.
But she can’t do any work now. Either I don’t understand, or you don’t want to understand me. She’s no good for work, she can only sleep or sit about.
I’ve grown ten years older tonight.
Goes to the cupboard and stands in the corner.
He hadn’t touched a drop for two years, and now he suddenly goes and gets drunk.﻿ ﻿…
Let’s sit down here. Nobody will come in here.
It’s past three now. It’s dawning.
They keep on asking me to get up a concert in aid of the sufferers.
As if one could do anything.﻿ ﻿…
It might be arranged, if necessary. In my opinion Maria Sergeyevna is an excellent pianist.
She’s forgotten everything. She hasn’t played for three years﻿ ﻿… or four.
In this town absolutely nobody understands music, not a soul except myself, but I do understand it, and assure you on my word of honour that Maria Sergeyevna plays excellently, almost with genius.
You are right, Baron, I’m awfully fond of Masha. She’s very fine.
To be able to play so admirably and to realize at the same time that nobody, nobody can understand you!
I heard so, too. Well, if it is so, the town will be quite empty.
Drops the clock which breaks to pieces.
A pause; everybody is pained and confused.
That clock used to belong to our mother.

Yes. Laughs. How strange everything really is! Pause. When the fire broke out, I hurried off home; when I get there I see the house is whole, uninjured, and in no danger, but my two girls are standing by the door in just their underclothes, their mother isn’t there, the crowd is excited, horses and dogs are running about, and the girls’ faces are so agitated, terrified, beseeching, and I don’t know what else. My heart was pained when I saw those faces. My God, I thought, what these girls will have to put up with if they live long! I caught them up and ran, and still kept on thinking the one thing: what they will have to live through in this world! Fire-alarm; a pause. I come here and find their mother shouting and angry. Masha enters with a pillow and sits on the sofa. And when my girls were standing by the door in just their underclothes, and the street was red from the fire, there was a dreadful noise, and I thought that something of the sort used to happen many years ago when an enemy made a sudden attack, and looted, and burned.﻿ ﻿… And at the same time what a difference there really is between the present and the past! And when a little more time has gone by, in two or three hundred years perhaps, people will look at our present life with just the same fear, and the same contempt, and the whole past will seem clumsy and dull, and very uncomfortable, and strange. Oh, indeed, what a life there will be, what a life! Laughs. Forgive me, I’ve dropped into philosophy again. Please let me continue. I do awfully want to philosophize, it’s just how I feel at present. Pause. As if they are all asleep. As I was saying: what a life there will be! Only just imagine.﻿ ﻿… There are only three persons like yourselves in the town just now, but in future generations there will be more and more, and still more, and the time will come when everything will change and become as you would have it, people will live as you do, and then you too will go out of date; people will be born who are better than you.﻿ ﻿… Laughs. Yes, today I am quite exceptionally in the vein. I am devilishly keen on living.﻿ ﻿… Sings.
“The power of love all ages know, From its assaults great good does grow.”
I don’t see anything funny about it. Is everything burnt?
No, you can’t come here, Vassili Vassilevitch. Please go away.
Why can the Baron come here and I can’t?
We really must go. How’s the fire?
Nicolai Lvovitch, go away from here.
Nicolai Lvovitch, go away! What business﻿ ﻿…
My dear Masha, my darling Masha.﻿ ﻿…
She’s tired out. You might let her rest, Fedia.
I’ll go at once. My wife’s a good, splendid﻿ ﻿… I love you, my only one.﻿ ﻿…
Amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant
What’s the use, Masha? Andrey is in debt all round; well, let him do as he pleases.
Don’t cry, dear girl, don’t cry﻿ ﻿… I suffer, too.
I’m not crying, not crying.﻿ ﻿… Enough.﻿ ﻿… Look, I’m not crying any more. Enough﻿ ﻿… enough!
I was always waiting until we should be settled in Moscow, there I should meet my true love; I used to think about him, and love him.﻿ ﻿… But it’s all turned out to be nonsense, all nonsense.﻿ ﻿…
Takes her head in her hands.
The firemen, sir, ask if they can go across your garden to the river. Else they go right round, right round; it’s a nuisance.
Walks about in silence, then stops.
It’s doctor Ivan Romanovitch. He’s drunk.
Then we shall be left alone.﻿ ﻿… Olga!

My dear, darling sister, I esteem, I highly value the Baron, he’s a splendid man; I’ll marry him, I’ll consent, only let’s go to Moscow! I implore you, let’s go! There’s nothing better than Moscow on earth! Let’s go, Olga, let’s go!

The old garden at the house of the Prosorovs. There is a long avenue of firs, at the end of which the river can be seen. There is a forest on the far side of the river. On the right is the terrace of the house: bottles and tumblers are on a table here; it is evident that champagne has just been drunk. It is midday. Every now and again passersby walk across the garden, from the road to the river; five soldiers go past rapidly.
It isn’t au revoir, it’s goodbye; we’ll never meet again!
We shall meet again, if God wills it. Write to us. Be sure to write.
We’d like to say goodbye to her.
They go aside and both look round.
Sits on the bottom step of the terrace.
And they forgot to say goodbye to me.
Puts one newspaper into his pocket and takes another out.
Yes, you ought to change your life, dear man, somehow or other.
We won’t reform Ivan Romanovitch! We won’t reform him!
If only I was apprenticed to you! Then I’d reform.
Feodor has shaved his moustache! I can’t bear to look at him.
I could tell you what your face looks like now, but it wouldn’t be polite.
Ivan Romanovitch, be a darling. I’m awfully worried. You were out on the boulevard last night; tell me, what happened?
They say that Soleni and the Baron met yesterday on the boulevard near the theatre.﻿ ﻿…
Waves his hand and goes into the house.
Near the theatre﻿ ﻿… Soleni started behaving offensively to the Baron, who lost his temper and said something nasty.﻿ ﻿…
I don’t know. It’s all bunkum.
Shouts of “Yo-ho!” are heard behind the stage.
Somehow or other, all this doesn’t seem at all serious. As if it was all ideas, and nothing really serious. Still, with all my soul I wish you happiness.
“The Maiden’s Prayer” is being played on the piano in the house.

No. She has been sent for. If you only knew how difficult it is for me to live alone, without Olga.﻿ ﻿… She lives at the high school; she, a headmistress, busy all day with her affairs and I’m alone, bored, with nothing to do, and hate the room I live in.﻿ ﻿… I’ve made up my mind: if I can’t live in Moscow, then it must come to this. It’s fate. It can’t be helped. It’s all the will of God, that’s the truth. Nicolai Lvovitch made me a proposal.﻿ ﻿… Well? I thought it over and made up my mind. He’s a good man﻿ ﻿… it’s quite remarkable how good he is.﻿ ﻿… And suddenly my soul put out wings, I became happy, and lighthearted, and once again the desire for work, work, came over me.﻿ ﻿… Only something happened yesterday, some secret dread has been hanging over me.﻿ ﻿…
“It is my washing day.﻿ ﻿… Tara-ra﻿ ﻿… boom-deay.”
Here you are, sitting here, doing nothing.
Is my man here? When our cook Martha used to ask about her gendarme, she used to say my man. Is he here?
When are they going to stop making such a noise in the house? It’s awful.
Winds the watch and makes it strike.
Somewhere a harp and violin are being played.
Everything’s all muddled up in my head.﻿ ﻿… But I say it ought not to be allowed. He might wound the Baron or even kill him.
Beyond the garden somebody shouts “Co-ee! Hallo!”
In my opinion it’s simply immoral to fight in a duel, or to be present, even in the quality of a doctor.
It only seems so.﻿ ﻿… We don’t exist, there’s nothing on earth, we don’t really live, it only seems that we live. Does it matter, anyway!
Our house will be empty. The officers will go away, you are going, my sister is getting married, and I alone will remain in the house.

A wife’s a wife. She’s honest, well-bred, yes; and kind, but with all that there is still something about her that degenerates her into a petty, blind, even in some respects misshapen animal. In any case, she isn’t a man. I tell you as a friend, as the only man to whom I can lay bare my soul. I love Natasha, it’s true, but sometimes she seems extraordinarily vulgar, and then I lose myself and can’t understand why I love her so much, or, at any rate, used to love her.﻿ ﻿…

The old man is unnecessarily excited. I won’t go far, I’ll only just bring him down like a snipe. Takes out his scent-bottle and scents his hands. I’ve poured out a whole bottle of scent today and they still smell﻿ ﻿… of a dead body. Pause. Yes.﻿ ﻿… You remember the poem
“But he, the rebel seeks the storm, As if the storm will bring him rest﻿ ﻿…”?
“He didn’t have the time to sigh, The bear sat on him heavily.”
He seems to be the only man in the town who is glad that the soldiers are going.
My dear, I shall return soon.
I must go into the town and then﻿ ﻿… see the others off.
Looking her closely in the face.
A shout of Co-ee! in the distance.
He goes quickly and stops in the avenue.
Andrey Sergeyevitch, it isn’t as if the documents were mine, they are the government’s. I didn’t make them.

The present is beastly, but when I think of the future, how good it is! I feel so light, so free; there is a light in the distance, I see freedom. I see myself and my children freeing ourselves from vanities, from kvass, from goose baked with cabbage, from after-dinner naps, from base idleness.﻿ ﻿…
He was saying that two thousand people were frozen to death. The people were frightened, he said. In Petersburg or Moscow, I don’t remember which.
Il ne faut pas faire du bruit, la Sophie est dormée deja. Vous êtes un ours.
At the window, nursing her boy.
Our garden might be a public thoroughfare, from the way people walk and ride across it. Nurse, give those musicians something!
The musicians bow and go away.
She’s somewhere in the garden. I’ll go and look for her.
If you’ll be so kind. I haven’t time.
Well﻿ ﻿… thank you for everything. Forgive me if I’ve﻿ ﻿… I’ve said such an awful lot﻿—forgive me for that too, don’t think badly of me.
Write to me.﻿ ﻿… Don’t forget! Let me go.﻿ ﻿… It’s time. Take her, Olga Sergeyevna﻿ ﻿… it’s time﻿ ﻿… I’m late﻿ ﻿…
“There stands a green oak by the sea, And a chain of bright gold is around it.﻿ ﻿… And a chain of bright gold is around it.﻿ ﻿…”
I’m going off my head﻿ ﻿… “There stands﻿ ﻿… a green oak﻿ ﻿… by the sea.”﻿ ﻿…
Don’t, Masha, don’t﻿ ﻿… give her some water.﻿ ﻿…
A shot is heard from a distance.
“There stands a green oak by the sea, And a chain of bright gold is around it﻿ ﻿… An oak of green gold.﻿ ﻿…”

I’m mixing it up.﻿ ﻿… Drinks some water. Life is dull﻿ ﻿… I don’t want anything more now﻿ ﻿… I’ll be all right in a moment.﻿ ﻿… It doesn’t matter.﻿ ﻿… What do those lines mean? Why do they run in my head? My thoughts are all tangled.
Be quiet, Masha. There’s a good girl.﻿ ﻿… Let’s go in.
Sobs, but controls herself at once.
He puts on the whiskers and beard.
You really do look like that German of yours.
A beautiful child, it’s quite true.
Going towards the house, to the maid.
A march is played off; they all listen.
I took them in﻿ ﻿… I’ll bring them, in a moment.
Yes, now we can all go home. It’s time.
The Baron was killed in the duel just now.
Sits on a bench at the back of the stage.
Takes a paper from his pocket.
Oh, how the music plays! They are leaving us, one has quite left us, quite and forever. We remain alone, to begin our life over again. We must live﻿ ﻿… we must live.﻿ ﻿…
If only we could know, if only we could know!
